claim: OptoFGFR1 is a photoactivatable version of FGFR1 that can be used to control Nlgn1 phosphorylation.
source: To acutely control Nlgn1 phosphorylation independently of endogenous ligand-activated kinases, we thus used here a photoactivatable version of FGFR1 (optoFGFR1) (Grusch et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: The text directly states the use of optoFGFR1 and cites a previous publication describing it.

claim: Light stimulation of optoFGFR1 induces Nlgn1 phosphorylation comparable to constitutively active FGFR1.
source: The stimulation of optoFGFR1 by light induced as much Nlgn1 phosphorylation as constitutively active FGFR1 (Figure 1C,D) (conditions CA and opto+, respectively), indicating potent kinase activation, while samples kept in the dark (conditions light-) did not show significant pTyr levels, revealing no unspecific effect of light.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1C,D comparing phosphorylation levels.

claim: Y782 is the only tyrosine residue on Nlgn1 phosphorylated by light-gated optoFGFR1.
source: Finally, no phosphorylation of the point mutant Nlgn1-Y782F was observed upon light application (Figure 1C,D), demonstrating that Y782 is the only tyrosine residue on Nlgn1 which is phosphorylated by light-gated optoFGFR1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no phosphorylation of the Y782F mutant.

claim: Light activation of optoFGFR1 for 24 hours increases dendritic spine density by approximately 25% in wild-type neurons.
source: Dendritic spine density increased by ~25% in neurons exposed to 470 nm light pulses for 24 hr, but remained stable in neurons expressing optoFGFR1 and kept in the dark, or in light-stimulated CA1 neurons from Nlgn1 KO slices (Figure 2C,D), demonstrating that this effect is mediated by light-dependent tyrosine phosphorylation of endogenous Nlgn1.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative spine density measurements shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The increase in dendritic spine density upon optoFGFR1 activation does not occur in Nlgn1 KO neurons.
source: Dendritic spine density increased by ~25% in neurons exposed to 470 nm light pulses for 24 hr, but remained stable in neurons expressing optoFGFR1 and kept in the dark, or in light-stimulated CA1 neurons from Nlgn1 KO slices (Figure 2C,D), demonstrating that this effect is mediated by light-dependent tyrosine phosphorylation of endogenous Nlgn1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing wild-type and Nlgn1 KO neurons.

claim: Light activation of optoFGFR1 increases evoked AMPAR-mediated EPSCs by approximately 200% compared to controls.
source: Strikingly, neurons expressing optoFGFR1 and exposed to light for 24 hr exhibited ~200% larger evoked AMPAR-mediated EPSCs compared to non-electroporated neighbors that also received light, or to neurons expressing optoFGFR1 and kept in the dark (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3D,F.

claim: Light activation of optoFGFR1 increases the frequency of spontaneous AMPAR-mediated EPSCs by almost two-fold.
source: This was accompanied by an almost two-fold increase in the frequency of spontaneous AMPAR-mediated EPSCs (Figure 3B,C), in agreement with the higher number of dendritic spines.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: OptoFGFR1 activation does not change AMPAR channel conductance.
source: No change in the amplitude or kinetics of spontaneous AMPAR-mediated EPSCs was measured (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), indicating that optoFGFR1 activation did not change AMPAR channel conductance.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of sEPSC amplitude and kinetics.

claim: Light activation of optoFGFR1 does not significantly affect evoked NMDAR-mediated EPSCs.
source: In parallel, there was no significant impact of optoFGFR1 expression and/or light on evoked NMDAR-mediated EPSCs (Figure 3E,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3E,G.

claim: The light-induced increase in AMPAR-mediated EPSCs is not observed in CA1 neurons from Nlgn1 KO slices.
source: Importantly, the light-induced increase AMPAR-mediated EPSCs was not observed in CA1 neurons from Nlgn1 KO slices (Figure 3D,F), demonstrating that this effect involves the selective tyrosine phosphorylation of Nlgn1.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data comparing wild-type and Nlgn1 KO neurons.

claim: OptoFGFR1 activation does not change the paired-pulse ratio, suggesting presynaptic function is unaltered.
source: The paired-pulse ratio was not changed by optoFGFR1 expression or light exposure, suggesting that presynaptic function was unaltered (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio measurements.

claim: OptoFGFR1 stimulation has no effect on inhibitory currents recorded in CA1 neurons.
source: Furthermore, although the critical tyrosine residue belonging to the gephyrin-binding motif is conserved in Nlgn2 and Nlgn3 (Poulopoulos et al., 2009), where it can also be phosphorylated (Letellier et al., 2018), no effect of optoFGFR1 stimulation was observed on inhibitory currents recorded in CA1 neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings of IPSCs.

claim: The phosphorylation mechanism is specific to the Nlgn1 isoform at excitatory post-synapses.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the phosphorylation mechanism is specific to the Nlgn1 isoform at excitatory post-synapses, and selectively affects AMPAR recruitment at pre-existing or newly formed spines.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined data showing specificity for Nlgn1 and excitatory synapses.

claim: The increase in spine density and AMPAR-mediated EPSCs by optoFGFR1 activation is not observed in CA1 neurons expressing Nlgn1-Y782F.
source: Importantly, the increase in spine density and AMPAR-mediated EPSCs by optoFGFR1 activation was not observed in CA1 neurons expressing Nlgn1-Y782F (Figure 4C,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that those effects are mediated by phosphorylation of the Nlgn1 Y782 residue induced by the photo-activation of optoFGFR1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments using the Y782F mutant shown in Figures 4C,E and supplement.

claim: CA1 neurons expressing optoFGFR1 and pre-exposed to light show a significant ~50% reduction in the LTP plateau level compared to control non-electroporated neighbors.
source: CA1 neurons expressing optoFGFR1 and pre-exposed to light showed a significant ~50% reduction in the LTP plateau level compared to control non-electroporated neighbors (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by LTP recordings shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Light stimulation of optoFGFR1 does not alter LTP in Nlgn1 KO neurons.
source: However, light stimulation of optoFGFR1 did not alter LTP in Nlgn1 KO neurons (Figure 5C,D), indicating that Nlgn1 phosphorylation is responsible for the decreased LTP in wild-type neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by LTP recordings in Nlgn1 KO neurons shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The LTP level in Nlgn1 KO neurons is barely reduced compared to wild-type.
source: To check if this effect was again specific of Nlgn1, we performed LTP experiments in hippocampal slices from Nlgn1 KO mice. Surprisingly, the LTP level was barely reduced (Figure 5A,C), despite a significant decrease in NMDA/AMPA ratio in control non-electroporated Nlgn1 KO neurons compared to neurons from WT mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Budreck et al., 2013; Chubykin et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by LTP recordings comparing wild-type and Nlgn1 KO neurons.

claim: Computer simulations of AMPAR diffusion-trapping match experimental LTP data in terms of kinetics and plateau value (~270%).
source: The simulations matched very well experimental LTP (Figure 5A,C), both in terms of kinetics and plateau value (~270%), supporting this diffusion/trap model.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data.

claim: Increasing the AMPAR/scaffold binding rate in simulations results in a ~2 fold increase of basal synaptic AMPAR number, reproducing experimental data.
source: To mimic the effect of Nlgn1 phosphorylation on postsynaptic density (PSD) assembly and AMPAR recruitment (Letellier et al., 2018), we raised the AMPAR/scaffold binding rate, resulting in a ~2 fold increase of basal synaptic AMPAR number (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) reproducing the experimental data (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results matching experimental observations.

claim: The partial occlusion of LTP upon optoFGFR1 stimulation can be explained by high initial recruitment of synaptic AMPARs, which depletes the extra-synaptic AMPAR reservoir necessary for LTP.
source: Thus, the partial occlusion of LTP observed upon optoFGFR1 stimulation can be explained by a high initial recruitment of synaptic AMPARs, which depletes the extra-synaptic AMPAR reservoir necessary for LTP.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on simulation results and experimental data.

claim: The model predicts a negative correlation between basal synaptic AMPAR number and the ability to respond to LTP.
source: Overall, our model predicts a negative correlation between basal synaptic AMPAR number and the ability to respond to LTP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), that perfectly fits the experiments (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation predictions that match experimental observations.

claim: Nlgn1 tyrosine phosphorylation impairs LTP by promoting high initial synaptic AMPAR levels.
source: These data suggest that Nlgn1 tyrosine phosphorylation impairs LTP by promoting high initial synaptic AMPAR levels.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined experimental and simulation data.

claim: Unphosphorylated Y782 strongly binds gephyrin.
source: This residue belongs to the gephyrin-binding motif and previous experiments showed that unphosphorylated Y782 strongly binds gephyrin - as does a Y782F mutant - while phosphorylated Y782 weakly binds gephyrin, a behavior phenocopied by a Y782A mutant (Giannone et al., 2013; Letellier et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Phosphorylated Y782 weakly binds gephyrin.
source: This residue belongs to the gephyrin-binding motif and previous experiments showed that unphosphorylated Y782 strongly binds gephyrin - as does a Y782F mutant - while phosphorylated Y782 weakly binds gephyrin, a behavior phenocopied by a Y782A mutant (Giannone et al., 2013; Letellier et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Neuronal expression of Nlgn1 Y782A promotes dendritic spine density and recruitment of PSD-95 and AMPARs.
source: In parallel, neuronal expression of Nlgn1 Y782A (but not Y782F) promotes dendritic spine density and recruitment of PSD-95 and AMPARs (Giannone et al., 2013; Letellier et al., 2018), suggesting that Nlgn1 tyrosine phosphorylation is responsible for these effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Nlgn1 overexpression or knockdown bi-directionally affect synapse number.
source: Specifically, whereas Nlgn OE or KD bi-directionally affect synapse number, full or conditional Nlgn1/2/3 KO does not alter synapse density (Chanda et al., 2017; Chih et al., 2005; Levinson et al., 2005; Prange et al., 2004; Varoqueaux et al., 2006), suggesting that Nlgns are not generally required for synaptogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Full or conditional Nlgn1/2/3 KO does not alter synapse density.
source: Specifically, whereas Nlgn OE or KD bi-directionally affect synapse number, full or conditional Nlgn1/2/3 KO does not alter synapse density (Chanda et al., 2017; Chih et al., 2005; Levinson et al., 2005; Prange et al., 2004; Varoqueaux et al., 2006), suggesting that Nlgns are not generally required for synaptogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Neurons might compete with one another for synapse formation, depending on their intrinsic Nlgn1 level.
source: To address this apparent conflict, experiments that mixed wild type and Nlgn1 KO neurons suggested the interesting model that neurons might compete with one another for synapse formation, depending on their intrinsic Nlgn1 level (Kwon et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Constitutive or conditional Nlgn1/2/3 KO selectively affect basal NMDAR-mediated EPSCs and not AMPAR-mediated EPSCs.
source: However, constitutive or conditional Nlgn1/2/3 KO selectively affect basal NMDAR-mediated EPSCs and not AMPAR-mediated EPSCs, and rescue experiments with truncated Nlgn1 mutants suggest that the synaptic recruitment of NMDARs requires the intracellular domain of Nlgn1 (Chanda et al., 2017; Chubykin et al., 2007; Jiang et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation (LTP) is impaired by Nlgn1 KD or KO.
source: Finally, while it is generally accepted that NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation (LTP) is impaired by Nlgn1 KD or KO, the issues of which Nlgn1 motifs are important in this process and whether the Nlgn1-NMDAR interaction is required, are unclear (Jiang et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2008; Letellier et al., 2018; Shipman and Nicoll, 2012; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Nlgn1 can be mislocalized at inhibitory synapses when overexpressed.
source: Furthermore, these techniques operate on a long-term basis, that is days to weeks, due to slow protein turnover. Hence, there is a pressing need for alternative paradigms allowing for an acute control of neuroligin signaling pathways (Jeong et al., 2017) without affecting its expression level.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing mislocalization.

claim: In its tyrosine phosphorylated state, Nlgn1 preferentially recruits intracellular PDZ domain containing scaffolding proteins including PSD-95.
source: Together, our results support a mechanism by which, in its tyrosine phosphorylated state, Nlgn1 preferentially recruits intracellular PDZ domain containing scaffolding proteins including PSD-95 (Giannone et al., 2013; Jeong et al., 2019), associated with a morphological stabilization of dendritic spines (Cane et al., 2014) and serving as slots for the diffusional trapping of surface AMPARs (Czöndör et al., 2013; Haas et al., 2018; Mondin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and the current experimental data.

claim: NMDAR-mediated EPSCs are not affected by Nlgn1 phosphorylation, supporting the concept of a direct extracellular coupling between Nlgn1 and GluN1.
source: In contrast, NMDAR-mediated EPSCs are not affected by Nlgn1 phosphorylation, supporting the concept of a direct extracellular coupling between Nlgn1 and GluN1 (Budreck et al., 2013; Shipman and Nicoll, 2012).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data supported by citations.

claim: PSD-95 overexpression increases spine density, enhances AMPAR- but not NMDAR-dependent transmission, and occludes LTP.
source: Importantly, optogenetic Nlgn1 phosphorylation induces a similar response as PSD-95 overexpression by increasing spine density, enhancing AMPAR- but not NMDAR-dependent transmission, and occluding LTP (Ehrlich and Malinow, 2004; El-Husseini et al., 2000; Stein et al., 2003), which further supports our model.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hippocampal LTP primarily involves the capture of extra-synaptic AMPARs.
source: This model is in line with experiments showing that hippocampal LTP primarily involves the capture of extra-synaptic AMPARs (Granger et al., 2013; Penn et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PKA-mediated phosphorylation of the S839 residue in Nlgn1 dynamically regulates PSD-95 binding, affecting both dendritic spine number and AMPAR-mediated miniature EPSCs.
source: A strong role of Nlgn1/PSD-95 interaction in synaptic function is also supported by a recent study showing that PKA-mediated phosphorylation of the S839 residue located near the C-terminal PDZ domain binding motif dynamically regulates PSD-95 binding, affecting both dendritic spine number and AMPAR-mediated miniature EPSCs (Jeong et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: OptoFGFR1 is lacking a ligand-binding domain, so its light-activation is expected to by-pass the endogenous regulation of Nlgn1 tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: Because optoFGFR1 is lacking a ligand-binding domain, its light-activation is expected to by-pass the endogenous regulation of Nlgn1 tyrosine phosphorylation, which involves the Trk family of tyrosine kinases (Letellier et al., 2018) that are responding to intrinsic ligands (BDNF and NGF) (Harward et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the structure of optoFGFR1 and citations to previous work.

claim: The endogenous regulation of Nlgn1 tyrosine phosphorylation involves the Trk family of tyrosine kinases.
source: Because optoFGFR1 is lacking a ligand-binding domain, its light-activation is expected to by-pass the endogenous regulation of Nlgn1 tyrosine phosphorylation, which involves the Trk family of tyrosine kinases (Letellier et al., 2018) that are responding to intrinsic ligands (BDNF and NGF) (Harward et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Trk family kinases respond to intrinsic ligands BDNF and NGF.
source: Because optoFGFR1 is lacking a ligand-binding domain, its light-activation is expected to by-pass the endogenous regulation of Nlgn1 tyrosine phosphorylation, which involves the Trk family of tyrosine kinases (Letellier et al., 2018) that are responding to intrinsic ligands (BDNF and NGF) (Harward et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Compensatory expression of Nlgn3 in Nlgn1 KO may explain why AMPAR-mediated EPSCs are not altered in the Nlgn1 KO.
source: The fact that AMPAR-mediated EPSCs are not altered in the Nlgn1 KO (Chanda et al., 2017) may result from the compensatory expression of scaffolding or adhesion molecules, in particular Nlgn3 (Dang et al., 2018), which also interacts with PSD-95.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A dual Nlgn1/3 KO is required to alter AMPARs levels and AMPAR-mEPSCs in cultured neurons.
source: This would explain the fact that a dual Nlgn1/3 (and triple Nlgn1/2/3) KO are required to alter AMPARs levels and AMPAR-mEPSCs in cultured neurons (Chanda et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: An optimal level of intracellular Nlgn1 tyrosine phosphorylation is necessary to elicit normal LTP.
source: Finally, increasing the Nlgn1 phosphorylation by optoFGFR1 activation reduced LTP, as did the expression of the non-phosphorylatable Nlgn1-Y782F mutant (Letellier et al., 2018), suggesting that an optimal level of intracellular Nlgn1 tyrosine phosphorylation is necessary to elicit normal LTP.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of experimental data and previous findings.

claim: LTP is impaired in acute slices from Nlgn1/2/3 cKO and can be rescued upon expression of a GPI-anchored Nlgn1 lacking the entire intracellular domain.
source: In contrast, another study found that LTP is impaired in acute slices from Nlgn1/2/3 cKO and can be rescued upon expression of a GPI-anchored Nlgn1 lacking the entire intracellular domain (Wu et al., 2019), and thus the C-terminal PDZ domain binding motif which we find important for anchoring AMPARs through PSD-95 (Letellier et al., 2018; Mondin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The optogenetic approach allows for an acute control of Nlgn1 signaling mechanisms.
source: This optogenetic strategy highlights the impact of Nlgn1 intracellular signaling in synaptic differentiation and potentiation, while enabling an acute control of these mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement about the advantages of the optogenetic approach.

claim: Nlgn1 intracellular signaling has an impact on synaptic differentiation and potentiation.
source: This optogenetic strategy highlights the impact of Nlgn1 intracellular signaling in synaptic differentiation and potentiation, while enabling an acute control of these mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Nlgn1 is important for regulating dendritic spine number.
source: Together, our results show that not only Nlgn1 is important for regulating dendritic spine number, but also that the Nlgn1 intracellular domain mediates AMPAR recruitment in basal conditions and regulates LTP.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The Nlgn1 intracellular domain mediates AMPAR recruitment in basal conditions.
source: Together, our results show that not only Nlgn1 is important for regulating dendritic spine number, but also that the Nlgn1 intracellular domain mediates AMPAR recruitment in basal conditions and regulates LTP.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The Nlgn1 intracellular domain regulates LTP.
source: Together, our results show that not only Nlgn1 is important for regulating dendritic spine number, but also that the Nlgn1 intracellular domain mediates AMPAR recruitment in basal conditions and regulates LTP.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: OptoFGFR1 contains a light-oxygen voltage sensing (LOV) domain fused to the C-terminus.
source: In this construct, the extracellular FGF binding domain has been removed, and a light-oxygen voltage sensing (LOV) domain is fused to the C-terminus, such that stimulation with blue light induces dimerization of the FGFR1 intracellular domain and subsequent kinase activation in a ligand-independent manner.
evidence: The claim describes the structure of the optoFGFR1 construct.

claim: Stimulation with blue light induces dimerization of the FGFR1 intracellular domain and subsequent kinase activation in a ligand-independent manner.
source: In this construct, the extracellular FGF binding domain has been removed, and a light-oxygen voltage sensing (LOV) domain is fused to the C-terminus, such that stimulation with blue light induces dimerization of the FGFR1 intracellular domain and subsequent kinase activation in a ligand-independent manner.
evidence: The claim describes the mechanism of optoFGFR1 activation.

claim: HA-tagged optoFGFR1 is detected throughout dendrites including spines.
source: Immunostained HA-tagged optoFGFR1 was detected throughout dendrites including spines, that is at the right location to phosphorylate Nlgn1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The increase in frequency of spontaneous AMPAR-mediated EPSCs indicates the formation of synapses containing a fixed bolus of AMPARs.
source: The increase in frequency - but not amplitude - of spontaneous AMPAR-mediated EPSCs upon optoFGFR1 stimulation indicates the formation of synapses containing a fixed bolus of AMPARs.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the electrophysiological data.

claim: Unphosphorylated Nlgn1 might associate with gephyrin clusters shown to dynamically appear and disappear on the sides of dendritic spines.
source: Conversely, unphosphorylated Nlgn1 (as mimicked by the Y782F mutant) might associate instead with gephyrin clusters shown to dynamically appear and disappear on the sides of dendritic spines (Villa et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: By locally controlling Nlgn1 phosphorylation, a single spine might have the possibility to assemble either excitatory or inhibitory scaffolding nanomodules.
source: Thus, by locally controlling Nlgn1 phosphorylation, a single spine might have the possibility to assemble either excitatory or inhibitory scaffolding nanomodules (Haas et al., 2018; Hruska et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The tyrosine residue in Nlgn1 belongs to a gephyrin-binding motif which is highly conserved among the other Nlgn isoforms.
source: Although the tyrosine residue in Nlgn1 belongs to a gephyrin-binding motif which is highly conserved among the other Nlgn isoforms and controls gephyrin binding (Giannone et al., 2013; Poulopoulos et al., 2009), optoFGFR1 stimulation did not affect evoked inhibitory currents, suggesting that the phosphorylation of Nlgn2 or Nlgn3 either did not occur, or did not modify the recruitment of the gephyrin scaffold and associated GABAA receptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The lack of effects of optoFGFR1 stimulation in neurons from Nlgn1 KO slices confirms that it is Nlgn1 phosphorylation which is causing the observed increases in dendritic spine density and AMPAR-mediated EPSCs.
source: The lack of effects of optoFGFR1 stimulation in neurons from Nlgn1 KO slices confirms that it is indeed Nlgn1 phosphorylation which is causing the observed increases in dendritic spine density and AMPAR-mediated EPSCs.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data from Nlgn1 KO experiments.

claim: The optogenetic phosphorylation of Nlgn1 provides the exciting opportunity to control in time and space synaptic connectivity and function.
source: Besides clarifying the role of Nlgn1 at excitatory synapses, the optogenetic phosphorylation of Nlgn1 provides the exciting opportunity to control in time and space synaptic connectivity and function, and has therefore a great potential for investigating the causality between synaptic plasticity and learning processes as well as the possible contribution of Nlgns to neuropsychiatric behaviors (Bourgeron, 2015).
evidence: The claim is a statement about the potential applications of the optogenetic approach.

claim: There is a significant decrease in NMDA/AMPA ratio in control non-electroporated Nlgn1 KO neurons compared to neurons from WT mice.
source: Surprisingly, the LTP level was barely reduced (Figure 5A,C), despite a significant decrease in NMDA/AMPA ratio in control non-electroporated Nlgn1 KO neurons compared to neurons from WT mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Budreck et al., 2013; Chubykin et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and citations.

claim: LTP is blocked by the NMDAR antagonist AP5.
source: Using a pairing protocol, we induced an increase of about threefold in evoked AMPAR-mediated EPSCs, which was blocked by the NMDAR antagonist AP5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There are about 30 AMPARs per synapse at basal state in control conditions.
source: With the chosen parameters however, there are about 30 AMPARs per synapse at basal state in control conditions, close to experimental measurements made by super-resolution imaging and freeze-fracture EM (Levet et al., 2015; Shinohara et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results matching experimental measurements from cited studies.

claim: CamKII activation increases the affinity of TARPs to PSD-95.
source: To simulate LTP, the AMPAR/scaffold unbinding rate (koff) was decreased at time zero from higher (0.02 to 0.08 s−1) to lower values (0.002–0.006 s−1), hereby mimicking a higher affinity of TARPs to PSD-95 induced by CamKII activation (Hafner et al., 2015; Opazo et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Expression of the non-phosphorylatable Nlgn1-Y782F mutant reduces LTP.
source: Finally, increasing the Nlgn1 phosphorylation by optoFGFR1 activation reduced LTP, as did the expression of the non-phosphorylatable Nlgn1-Y782F mutant (Letellier et al., 2018), suggesting that an optimal level of intracellular Nlgn1 tyrosine phosphorylation is necessary to elicit normal LTP.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Expression of Nlgn1 Y782A almost completely occludes LTP.
source: Accordingly, we previously reported an almost complete occlusion of LTP upon replacement of endogenous Nlgn1 by a Y782A mutant which phenocopies maximally phosphorylated Nlgn1 and increases AMPAR-mediated EPSCs by ~4 fold (Giannone et al., 2013; Letellier et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Nlgn1 Y782A mutant increases AMPAR-mediated EPSCs by ~4 fold.
source: Accordingly, we previously reported an almost complete occlusion of LTP upon replacement of endogenous Nlgn1 by a Y782A mutant which phenocopies maximally phosphorylated Nlgn1 and increases AMPAR-mediated EPSCs by ~4 fold (Giannone et al., 2013; Letellier et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Several tyrosine kinases including Trk family receptors and FGFR1 can directly phosphorylate Nlgn1.
source: Using an in vitro kinase assay on recombinant GST fused to the intracellular domain of Nlgn1, we previously identified several tyrosine kinases able to directly phosphorylate Nlgn1, including Trk family receptors and the FGFR1 (Letellier et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.
